_meta: The same five values presented in two different input arrangements, sorted with a 'within tolerance' comparator, used to show that a comparator must define a consistent total order or the sort result is not even well-defined -- it depends on the input arrangement and is not reproducible. A tempting comparator treats two values as equal when they are within a tolerance and otherwise orders them by value: cmp(a,b) = 0 if abs(a-b) <= eps else sign(a-b). It looks reasonable and it is a real bug, because the 'equal' relation it defines is not transitive: with eps=10, 0 is within tolerance of 6 and 6 is within tolerance of 12, so the comparator calls 0 and 6 equal and 6 and 12 equal, yet 0 and 12 are 12 apart and it calls them unequal. A sort needs the comparison to be a total order -- transitive and consistent -- to place elements unambiguously; a non-transitive comparator gives the sort no consistent target, so the order it lands on depends on how the elements were arranged going in, and the same multiset can come out ascending from one arrangement and descending from another, each 'sorted' in the sense that every adjacent pair is within tolerance. Java's TimSort even throws 'Comparison method violates its general contract' when it detects this. The fix is a comparator that is a genuine total order: compare the exact values (order by value, break ties by an exact key), which sorts the same multiset to the same sequence regardless of input arrangement. eps is the tolerance; arrangement_a and arrangement_b are two orderings of the identical multiset. The two comparators' outputs on each arrangement, and whether each is reproducible, are computed. Stdlib only.
